name: Omar Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the farm lead at Greenbank, which is a worker co-operative, so the nine of us who work it also own it together. We've got 70 suckler cows, that's beef cows raising their own calves, 400 ewes, and potatoes and oats on about 180 hectares. My day starts at six with the stock round on the quad bike, then a quick meeting in the old dairy with whoever's on, and then it's the job of the season. Right now it's lifting the last potatoes and getting the tups, the rams, out with the ewes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy that when we decide something, we all decide it, round the kitchen table with a pot of tea. I like a good lambing, when the shed is full and nothing goes wrong for a night. What wears me down is the supermarket potato contract, because every year they want the same spuds a bit bigger, a bit cleaner, for a bit less. Mei, my wife, says I come home from those calls looking ten years older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, the hype was overblown, and the real story in farming was always prices and weather. At the co-op meeting I'd say let's stop reading AI headlines and start reading the potato contract. I might post something about how farm workers are still the backbone of food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't change our biggest problem, which is that one supermarket buys most of our potatoes and sets the price. If they squeeze us another few percent, Greenbank's margin goes, and my pay is the co-op's margin. With a mortgage and two kids, that's what keeps me up, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the farm running the way it is, it works. I'd go to the other two potato co-ops in the valley and propose we negotiate the supermarket contract together next spring, so they can't pick us off one by one. And I'd keep using the co-op's grazing app now and then, because it does save me a walk on wet days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit flat, because the hard stuff is still hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your pay is the co-op's margin. What happens at home if the contract drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd take less from the co-op for a season, all nine of us, that's how it works. At home, it's the kids' swimming club and the second car that go first. Mei's nursing pay covers the mortgage, which is a blessing, but I hate that it has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the other co-ops to get them on board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them a supermarket can drop one small co-op and never notice, but three co-ops growing a third of the valley's potatoes is a supplier they can't ignore. We share a tractor ring already, so we can share a negotiator. It's the same idea that started Greenbank in the first place.

say: I'd say the **hype was overblown** and farming is still about prices and weather.
I'd post that **farm workers** are still the backbone of the food system.
think: One **supermarket** sets most of our potato price, and that's my real worry.
My pay is the **co-op's margin**, so a few percent off the contract hits home.
do: Keep **running Greenbank** as it is, because the system works.
Propose a **joint contract talk** with the valley's two other potato co-ops next spring.
Keep using the **grazing app** now and then on wet days.
feel: **Mostly fine**, but flat, because the hard parts of farming stay hard.
S0.quote: A supermarket can drop one small co-op and never notice, but three co-ops growing a third of the valley's potatoes is a supplier they can't ignore.
fieldNote: His worry is **buyer power**, not technology.
Thinks naturally in **collective terms**: the co-op, the valley, shared negotiators.
Admits **Mei's nursing pay** carries the mortgage in bad years, and it bothers him.
Uses AI tools **casually**, only where they save effort.

steps.text: Keep running Greenbank's cattle, sheep and potatoes as now
Propose joint potato contract talks with the valley's two other co-ops
Keep using the co-op grazing app on wet days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where co-ops have the edge, because when we bring in a new tool we decide together who it helps. I'd tell people at the market that AI doing the planning and paperwork is fine, as long as the gains go to workers. Online I'd probably argue for rules on how supermarkets use AI to set prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's mostly good for Greenbank. The paperwork, the subsidy forms, the crop plans, the ordering, that's half a day a week for me, and I'd happily give it to a computer. My worry is the supermarket's buyers having AI that knows our costs better than we do, and using it to squeeze us harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a farm I know had used something for a full season, then bring it to the co-op meeting. If the robot weeder at the Ashby estate works on their potatoes, I'd propose we buy one between the three valley co-ops. I'd also do a short course on using AI for crop planning, because if we don't understand it, the supermarket will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Interested, even. It's the first one that sounds like we'd have a say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the supermarket might know your costs better than you. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A supermarket buyer with AI would phone me with an offer exactly one penny above what Greenbank can survive on. They already guess at it, but with AI they'd know. That's why I'd want our own numbers sharper than theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the co-op would find this hardest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jen, who's done our books for twelve years and does them by hand in a big green ledger. If the software does that, she'd need something else to do. We'd find her a place, probably running the farm shop idea we keep talking about, because that's the point of owning it together.

say: I'd say **co-ops have the edge** because members decide who new tools help.
I'd argue for **rules** on how supermarkets use AI to set prices.
think: Handing **paperwork and ordering** to a computer would free half a day a week.
The danger is the **supermarket's AI** knowing our costs and squeezing us harder.
do: Wait for a **full season** of proof on a neighbour's farm before buying anything.
Propose a **shared robot weeder** with the valley co-ops if Ashby's works.
Take a short course on **AI crop planning** this winter.
feel: **Steady** and quietly interested, because the co-op would have a say.
S1.quote: A supermarket buyer with AI would phone me with an offer exactly one penny above what Greenbank can survive on.
fieldNote: He sees **AI on paperwork** as a gain for a co-op, not a threat.
His real fear shifts to **pricing power** in the buyer's hands.
Classic steady adopter: waits for a **neighbour's full season** before buying.
Thinks about **Jen the bookkeeper** and plans to protect her role.

steps.text: Wait for a full season of results from Ashby's robot weeder
Propose buying one robot weeder between the three valley co-ops
Take a winter course on using AI for crop planning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for public ownership and strong rules, because if this hits in two years, the big landowners and food companies will grab everything. I'd be writing to our member of parliament about a robot tax that pays for retraining and a basic income. At the co-op, I'd say we need to meet every week, not every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the thinking side lands on us in 2028 and that's fine, it's not most of our work. The robots in 2031 are the problem. Big farms with robot fleets will grow potatoes cheaper than nine people ever can, and the supermarket will buy from them. Greenbank could go under by 2032, and I'd be 49 with a mortgage and a degree in a job that doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the co-op to start saving a robot fund now, so we can buy machines ourselves before the price war rather than be crushed by it. At home, Mei and I would freeze anything big, no kitchen extension, and pay the mortgage down harder. I'd also talk to the bank about what happens if our income drops by half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because we'd have three years to move, and because there are nine of us. But anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Yusuf, who's 14, about his own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Yusuf not to pick a career by asking what's safe, because nobody knows. I'd tell him to learn how the machines work and how money works, and to stay close to people who'll stand with him. That's all I really know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said both that you'd buy robots and that you'd campaign against the people who'll own them. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They fit fine to me. If robots are coming, I'd rather nine workers own them than one investor. That's not against robots, it's about who owns the field and the machine in it.

say: I'd call for **public ownership** and strong rules before landowners grab everything.
I'd write to our MP about a **robot tax** funding retraining and basic income.
think: Thinking AI in 2028 is fine, but **robots in 2031** let big farms undercut us.
Greenbank could **go under by 2032**, leaving me at 49 with a mortgage.
do: Ask the co-op to start a **robot fund** now, before any price war.
Freeze the **kitchen extension** and pay the mortgage down harder.
Write to the MP about a **robot tax** this year.
feel: **Anxious**, but not panicked, because there are three years and nine of them.
S2.quote: If robots are coming, I'd rather nine workers own them than one investor.
fieldNote: Sees the **three-year robot gap** as the co-op's window to buy in.
Squares progressive politics with automation through **worker ownership**.
Household cushion is **Mei's nursing job** plus moderate savings.
Advice to his son is about **solidarity and skills**, not a safe job.

steps.text: Ask Greenbank's members to start a robot fund this year
Freeze the kitchen extension and overpay the mortgage
Write to the local MP backing a robot tax for retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the co-op movement to get organised, if we start now. I'd go round the farming co-ops in the region and say let's buy robots together and share the engineers. I'd say it in the papers if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm less worried with five years. 2031 for the thinking work, 2034 for robots, that gives Greenbank time to raise money and learn. I'd be 51 when the robots come, still young enough to learn to run them, and the kids would be mostly grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep farming as normal but take a part-time course in farm robotics at the agricultural college, one day a week over the winter. I'd ask the co-op to put a share of every year's profit into a machine fund. And I'd push the regional co-op federation to set up a shared robot pool, the way we share tractors now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more energised than scared. It feels like a job to be done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you're running robots, who does the work you do now, the stock round, the lambing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it the robots, I suppose, and some of it still us, because a ewe in trouble at 3am needs judgement as much as hands. I can see myself checking the robots in the morning and doing the hard lambings at night. Less sweat, more screens, but still a farmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mei say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei would say I've finally found a reason to go back to college. She'd also ask if the hospital is next, because nursing robots are part of the same story. We'd both be learning, I think.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough for co-ops to get organised if we start now.
I'd tell regional co-ops to **buy robots together** and share engineers.
think: With robots in **2034**, I'd be 51, young enough to learn to run them.
Five years gives Greenbank time to **raise money** and learn the machines.
do: Take a weekly **farm robotics course** at the agricultural college this winter.
Ask the co-op to put a **share of profit** into a machine fund every year.
Push the regional federation for a **shared robot pool**.
feel: **Uneasy** but energised, like a big job waiting to be done.
S3.quote: A ewe in trouble at 3am needs judgement as much as hands.
fieldNote: The extra years turn his fear into an **organising plan**.
Pictures a **mixed future**: robots by day, hard lambings by night.
Notes his wife's **nursing job** is also exposed, so both would retrain.
Steady pace fits: a **part-time course**, not a leap.

steps.text: Take a one-day-a-week farm robotics course at the agricultural college
Ask Greenbank to put a yearly share of profit into machines
Push the regional co-op federation to set up a shared robot pool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd say the same thing I always say, which is that the question is who owns the machines. At the co-op I'd put it on the agenda once a year, not every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 53 when the robots arrive, with the mortgage nearly done and both kids grown. That's a decent position. I'd probably let the young members lead the robot side and stay on as the stockman they come to when the machine doesn't know what it's looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change very little in year one. I'd keep using the AI tools a bit more each year as they prove themselves, starting with the subsidy forms. I'd keep paying into my pension and the co-op's reserve, and watch what the big estates do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. A bit uneasy about the country, but not much about us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say calm about yourself. What about the country makes you uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough time for governments to talk and do nothing. I've seen that with farm policy my whole life. If the end point is the same, I'd want the rules written while it's still a fair fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a young person joining Greenbank in 2027?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a young person joining Greenbank to learn the animals from me and the machines from the college, because by 2039 they'll need both. And I'd tell them they own a share of whatever comes, so it's worth caring about.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it.
I'd repeat that the real question is **who owns** the machines.
think: At **53** with the mortgage nearly paid, I'd be in a decent position.
I'd let **young members** lead the robots while I stay the stockman.
do: Use **AI tools** a bit more each year, starting with subsidy forms.
Keep paying into my **pension** and the co-op's reserve.
Watch what the **big estates** do before changing anything.
feel: A bit **uneasy** that government will waste the decade.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time for governments to talk and do nothing. I've seen that with farm policy my whole life.
fieldNote: Personal worry is low; his unease is **political**, about wasted time.
Sees himself as the **mentor** while younger members run machines.
Steady approach: adopt **AI gradually**, starting with forms.
Ownership remains his **core theme** across every scenario.

steps.text: Hand the subsidy forms to an AI tool next year
Keep paying into his pension and the co-op reserve

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would come in 2031, before small co-ops could raise the money to own them. What would help is cheap public loans for co-ops and small farms to buy robots together, and a law that stops supermarkets using AI to see their suppliers' costs. Retraining at the college for people like Jen, too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who'll own the land. Robots on a field don't change who owns the field, and in this valley that's still five families and a pension fund. Whoever owns the land and the robots will own the farm, and everyone else will be visiting.

headlineQuote: Whoever owns the land and the robots will own the farm, and everyone else will be visiting.
portrait: **Omar Ito**, 43, is farm lead at Greenbank, a **worker co-op** of nine members with beef, sheep and potatoes.
His steady worry is a **supermarket contract** that sets his pay through the co-op's margin.
He picks up tools **once proven**, and sees AI paperwork as a gain.
Fast AGI scares him because **big robot farms** could undercut Greenbank by 2032.
His answer every time is **worker ownership** of machines, plus public loans and rules.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive before small co-ops can afford to own them.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap public loans** for co-ops to buy robots together.
A ban on supermarkets using AI to see **suppliers' costs**, plus college retraining.
